FIGURE 1
Characterization of various Cu interface layers. (a) Schematic illustration of zinc deposition on different Cu interfaces; SEM images of
(b) normal Cu and (e) modified Cu; Cross-sectional images of the FIB-HRTEM samples: (c) normal Cu and (f) modified Cu; Cross-sectional HRTEM
image of (d) normal Cu interface and (g) modified Cu interface.

FIGURE 2
Electrochemical performance of zinc plating/stripping process at various Cu interfaces, the related observation of zinc reaction and
the performance comparison. (a) Cycling performance of zinc plating/stripping CE under various parameters. (b) In situ optical microscopy about zinc
plating process at different Cu interfaces. (c) Performance comparison of our work with other reports in terms of ZRR, cumulative capacity, and current
density. Scale bar: b, 10 µm.

FIGURE 3
SEM images about zinc deposition of 0.5 mA cm−2/0.5 mAh cm−2 at (a) normal Cu and (b) modified Cu and 2 mA cm−2/2 mAh cm−2

FIGURE 4
Electrochemical analysis and simulations about HER at Cu interfaces. (a) LSV curves of various Cu samples in 1 m Na2SO4 electrolyte.
(b) EIS curves and (c) the derived DRT curve of various Cu interfaces. (d) H2 coevolution efficiency when zinc was plated at 2 mA cm−2. (e) Gibbs free
energies and hydrogen adsorption process at Cu interfaces, and (f) the related partial density of states (PDOS) of various Cu interfaces.

FIGURE 5
Electrochemical performance of full cell with limited zinc supply. (a) CV curves at 1 mV s−1 (dashed line for first cycle and solid line
for fourth cycle) and (b) rate performance of PVO//Cu-Zn full cells. (c) Schematic illustration of the full cell design with limited zinc supply. Cycling
performance of (d) PVO//Cu-Zn full cells and (e) PVO//Cu-Zn pouch cell at 8 mA cm−2. (f) Comparison of the energy density and areal capacity of Zn
metal full cells with previous reports.

Figure 5d, the cell using Zn anode deposited on modified Cu can
stably operate for 250 cycles at 1 A g−1, achieving a high energy
density of 188.3 Wh kg−1 at a low N/P ratio of 1.2 (83.3% ZUR). By
comparison, the cell employing normal Cu suffers a quick drop
in 50 cycles, and the cell with Zn foil (100 µm) gets short in 135
cycles, implying excess zinc is not essential for stability (Figures
S27 and S28). Furthermore, this host strategy was extended to
a 50 × 50 mm2 pouch cell with limited zinc (N/P = 1.6) for
assessment. The single-layer pouch cell reaches an areal capacity
of 2 mAh cm−2, and exhibits a capacity retention of 84% in 80
cycles (Figure 5e), underscoring the practical applications of the
engineered Cu interface. Compared with other state-of-the-art
works in pursuing zinc reaction reversibility, the PVO//Cu-Zn
full batteries achieve highest energy density at a practical areal
capacity in Figure 5f, highlighting the advantage of host-interface
design.
